draft.title: IUPAC naming
card: An IUPAC name is built in parts. The stem shows the number of carbons in the longest chain: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6).
The ending shows the functional group. Alkanes end in -ane, alkenes in -ene, alcohols in -ol and carboxylic acids in -oic acid.

Numbers show where a branch or functional group sits. Count from the end of the chain that gives the lowest numbers. A branch is named by its own stem with -yl, such as methyl, and goes in front of the main name.
Example: in 2-methylbutane, the main chain is 4 carbons (butane) and a methyl branch is on carbon 2. In butan-2-ol, the -OH group is on carbon 2 of a 4-carbon chain.
draft.remember: A name gives the chain length, the functional group, and the position of each branch or group.

a.q: What does the 'pent' in pentan-1-ol tell you?
opts: The longest chain has five carbons
There is a branch with five carbons
a.why: The stem pent shows a longest chain of five carbons. The position of the -OH group is shown by the number 1, not by the stem. Mixing up the stem with the position is a common mistake.
a.clue: The stem counts carbons in the longest chain.

b.q: A molecule has a 4-carbon chain with a single -OH group on carbon 2 and a methyl branch on carbon 3. Which name fits it?
b.why: The chain has four carbons, so it is butane, and the ending -ol shows the alcohol. The -OH group is on carbon 2 and the methyl branch on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-2-ol. 2-methylbutan-3-ol is tempting, but it swaps the positions and so numbers the chain from the wrong end.
b.clue: Name the chain, then place the -OH and the branch by number.

a.best: The longest chain has five carbons

problems.detail: Both 3-methylbutan-2-ol and 2-methylbutan-3-ol use the locants 2 and 3, so the card's only rule ('count from the end that gives the lowest numbers') cannot tell them apart. Choosing the right name needs the rule that the functional group (-OH) gets the lowest possible number before branches do, and the card never teaches it.

The numbering rule says only to give the lowest numbers. It leaves out that the functional group takes priority for the lowest number over branches, so a student following the card could wrongly accept 2-methylbutan-3-ol.

Numbers show where a branch or functional group sits. Number the chain from the end that gives the functional group the lowest number. Branches get the lowest numbers only when that still leaves a choice.
A branch is named by its own stem with -yl, such as methyl, and goes in front of the main name. In 2-methylbutane, a methyl branch sits on carbon 2 of a 4-carbon chain.

b.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH3?
b.why: The longest chain has four carbons, so it is butane with an -ol ending. Numbering from the end nearer the -OH puts it on carbon 2 and the methyl on carbon 3. 2-methylbutan-3-ol is tempting because it gives the branch a lower number, but the functional group takes priority.
b.clue: Which part of the molecule gets first claim on the lowest number?
